property_summary: For any caller context where proxiableUUID() is callable (does not revert) the reference implementation always returns the IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT constant while the mutant returns a different slot (ADMIN_SLOT) for some inputs, so their return values must differ for at least some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller context where proxiableUUID() does not revert, the correct contract always returns the IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT constant, whereas the mutant can return a different slot (ADMIN_SLOT) for some caller contexts — so the returned bytes32 must equal ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT for all inputs in the correct contract and the mutant will violate this for some input.

For every caller context (any caller address) the correct contract's proxiableUUID() returns ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT; the mutant returns a different constant (ADMIN_SLOT) for some caller addresses, so asserting the return equals IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT is a universal rule the reference satisfies and the mutant breaks for some fuzzed caller.

For any caller address, C.proxiableUUID() completes (does not revert) and returns the constant ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT; the mutant returns a different constant (ADMIN_SLOT) for some callers, violating this equality.

For every caller address that is an EOA (no code) the reference C.proxiableUUID() returns the IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT constant; the mutant returns a different constant (ADMIN_SLOT) for some caller addresses (when called as a non-delegated direct call) so asserting proxiableUUID()==ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT is a universal rule the reference satisfies and the mutant violates for some fuzzed caller addresses.

After calling initialize(...) the reference sets the UUPS proxiable UUID (proxiableUUID callable without reverting under notDelegated) by performing __UUPSUpgradeable_init(), so calling proxiableUUID via direct call on the implementation contract succeeds (not reverted) for all inputs; the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() causes proxiableUUID to revert (unauthorized call context) for some inputs, so the behavior differs.

For every input admin address, calling initialize(admin) on the correct contract always allows external calls to proxiableUUID() (i.e. it does not revert when called directly), whereas the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can cause proxiableUUID() to revert for some admin addresses (due to UUPS not being properly initialized).

For every input admin address, calling initialize(admin) on the correct contract (P) always completes successfully (does not revert) and allows calling proxiableUUID() without reverting (i.e. proxiableUUID can be called directly on the implementation), whereas the mutant (which omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init()) can make proxiableUUID() revert for some admin addresses—so the invariant is: initialize(...) then proxiableUUID() must be callable (not revert).

For any admin address passed to initialize, the reference C executes __UUPSUpgradeable_init() causing proxiableUUID() to be callable (not reverting) when invoked directly on the implementation; the mutant omitting __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can make proxiableUUID() revert for some admin addresses — we instead assert the more general rule that after initialize(admin) the implementation's proxiableUUID() returns the ERC1967 implementation slot (i.e. a specific bytes32) without reverting for all admin inputs, which the mutant breaks for some inputs.

For any caller address passed to initialize, the reference contract's initializer sets the contract into an initializing state such that a subsequent call to proxiableUUID() made directly on the implementation (i.e. not via delegatecall) does NOT revert; the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can leave the contract such that direct calls to proxiableUUID() revert for some inputs — we assert that calling initialize(...) always leaves proxiableUUID() callable (returns a bytes32) without revert.

After any successful call to initialize(...) the contract's initialized version (returned by calling the internal initializer observable via re-initialization attempt) prevents re-initialization: the reference records version 1 so a subsequent initializer call reverts, whereas the mutant sets _initialized to 2 allowing a second initialize() to behave differently (the rule: calling initialize twice must revert the second time), and the mutant breaks this for some inputs.

For every address used as the accessControl initializer, calling initialize(access) succeeds once and sets the contract into an initialized state that causes any subsequent call to initialize(access) (even from the same caller) to revert; the mutant incorrectly records version 2 causing the second initialize call made in construction-like or edge-case contexts to behave differently and thus may allow a second initialization attempt to succeed or change emitted state compared to the reference.

After calling initialize(...) once from an EOA, the contract should record that it has been initialized so that a subsequent call to initializer context (a direct external initialize call) reverts — the mutant that sets _initialized to 2 can break the reinitialization guard in certain construction-like conditions, so we assert that a second initialize call always reverts for any admin address.

After a successful external initialize(...) call made when the contract is not in a construction context, the reference C always marks itself as initialized so that calling proxiableUUID() via an external call that requires notDelegated/proxiable semantics reverts when called through the implementation (i.e. proxiableUUID() must be callable only not-delegated) — the mutant's wrong initialized flag can change the call context behavior and allow a proxiableUUID() call that should be disallowed, so the property checks that calling proxiableUUID() directly on the implementation (not via delegatecall) returns the expected ERC1967 slot and that an initialize then a proxiableUUID call from an external context behaves consistently; the mutant breaks this for some inputs.

For any caller address used as the accessControl argument, calling initialize(accessControl) once from an EOA always succeeds and sets the contract so that a subsequent external attempt to call initialize(accessControl) (i.e. a re-initialization) reverts; the mutant that writes _initialized = 2 breaks this invariant for some inputs because it changes the construction-vs-external initialization logic and can allow a second initialize call to succeed in certain fuzzed scenarios.

For any vault/address and any time elapsed >=0, C.rate returns the same value as calling _applySlopes with utilization measured as (index - previousIndex) divided by elapsed when elapsed>0; the mutant removes the division by elapsed so for some inputs (where elapsed>0 and index-change !=0) the returned rate differs.

For any vault, asset, previous index and elapsed time, C.rate returns the same value as calling _applySlopes with utilization computed as (index - previousIndex) / elapsed when elapsed>0 (i.e. utilization is a rate per second); the mutant removes division by elapsed so when elapsed>0 and index change != 0 the mutant yields a different returned rate.

For any vault, asset and prior stored utilization index/lastUpdate, if block time advances (elapsed > 0) then C.rate(...) computes utilization as (index - previousIndex) / elapsed and returns _applySlopes(..., utilization, elapsed); the mutant that omits division by elapsed will make C.rate(...) produce a different returned value for some fuzzed inputs (when elapsed>0 and index - previousIndex != 0).

For any vault/asset and stored prior utilization index and lastUpdate, if block.timestamp advances (elapsed > 0) then C.rate(...) computes utilization as (index - previousIndex) / elapsed (a per-second rate) and returns _applySlopes(..., utilization, elapsed); the mutant that omits the division by elapsed will cause a differing returned value for some fuzzed inputs (when elapsed>0 and index - previousIndex != 0).

For any vault/asset and stored prior utilization index/lastUpdate, if block.timestamp advances (elapsed > 0) then C.rate(...) returns the same value as calling _applySlopes with utilization computed as (index - previousIndex) / elapsed (i.e. utilization per-second); the mutant removing the division will cause a differing returned value for some inputs where elapsed>0 and index change != 0.

For any call to rate, if block.timestamp > lastUpdate then the utilization passed to _applySlopes equals (currentUtilizationIndex - stored index) / elapsed when elapsed != block.timestamp, and equals IVault.utilization when elapsed == block.timestamp; the mutant wrongly uses raw index difference when elapsed == block.timestamp causing a different returned rate for some inputs.

For any inputs, when calling rate(...) the reference contract always returns a value consistent with using IVault.utilization() whenever block.timestamp - lastUpdate == block.timestamp (i.e. lastUpdate == 0), whereas the mutant sometimes uses the raw index difference in that case and thus can produce a different return — so the property asserts that calling rate(...) does NOT revert and returns equal results if lastUpdate == 0 and currentUtilizationIndex and utilization are consistent; the mutant will violate this for some fuzzed inputs.

For any vault/asset and prior stored state where lastUpdate == 0, calling rate(...) should return the same value as when IVault.utilization(_asset) is used (i.e. the reference always uses IVault.utilization when lastUpdate==0), but the mutant may instead use the raw index difference and thus return a different value for some inputs.

For any vault, asset and stored utilization data, when lastUpdate == 0 the reference implementation of rate(...) always uses IVault.utilization(_asset) to compute the returned rate (so calling rate via the contract that forwards to an IVault that returns a specific utilization yields the same non-reverting result), whereas the mutant sometimes uses the raw index difference instead and thus can return a different value; the test asserts that calling rate does not revert and returns equal results compared to a direct call path that forces IVault.utilization to the same value the reference uses.

For any vault, asset and prior stored UtilizationData with lastUpdate == 0, calling rate(...) on the correct contract always calls IVault.utilization(_asset) to compute utilization (and thus returns a value consistent with that IVault.utilization), whereas the mutant may instead use the raw index difference when elapsed == block.timestamp (lastUpdate==0) and so can return a different value for some inputs.

For any call to rate, when block.timestamp > utilizationData.lastUpdate and elapsed == 0 the reference uses the index-based computation (index - prevIndex)/elapsed only when elapsed>0, otherwise it falls back to IVault.utilization; the mutant incorrectly overrides the index-based result when elapsed==0 causing rate to differ for some inputs (timestamps/index/lastUpdate) leading to different returned latestAnswer.

For any inputs, when C.rate(...) is called it must return the same value whether elapsed computed inside is zero or non-zero only when elapsed==0 the reference still uses IVault.utilization for utilization (so rate returns value consistent with the vault's utilization when elapsed==0); the mutant overrides a valid non-zero-index computation by forcing utilization = IVault.utilization when elapsed==0 causing rate to differ for some inputs.

For every call to rate(vault, asset) the reference contract computes utilization using the index-based delta whenever elapsed > 0 (and only falls back to IVault.utilization when elapsed == 0 or lastUpdate is not older than block.timestamp); the mutant sometimes overrides a legitimately computed index-based utilization when elapsed == 0 causing rate(...) to return a different value — the property asserts that whenever block.timestamp > stored lastUpdate and elapsed == 0 the contract still uses the vault-reported utilization (i.e., both branches produce the same observable rate in the reference), which the mutant can violate for some inputs.

For any vault, asset, prior index and lastUpdate, when calling c.rate(vault,asset) the reference implementation never returns a different rate due to an extra override that sets utilization to IVault(vault).utilization(asset) only when elapsed == 0; the mutant that force-overrides utilization when elapsed == 0 can make rate(...) return a different value for some inputs (timestamps and stored index) and thus violates this invariant.

For every call to c.rate(vault, asset) the reference contract never reverts and produces a result consistent with using IVault.currentUtilizationIndex delta when elapsed>0 and IVault.utilization when elapsed==0; the mutant that force-overrides utilization when elapsed==0 can make the returned latestAnswer differ, so there exists fuzzed inputs (vault index/lastUpdate/timestamp setup) where mutant's return != reference's return.

For any input slopes, the reference contract rejects a kink of 0 (reverting setSlopes) while the mutant accepts kink==0; therefore for all inputs P either reverts when kink==0 and never stores such a slope, whereas M will succeed and store kink==0 — the test fuzzes kink and asserts that setSlopes call success is false whenever kink==0 (a property P enforces, M violates).

For all inputs, the reference contract rejects (reverts) any SlopeData with kink == 0 when calling setSlopes; the mutant removes that zero check and therefore accepts (succeeds) for some inputs (kink == 0), violating the rule.
For every call to setSlopes, the reference contract always reverts (fails) when slopes.kink == 0; the mutant removes that check and will succeed for some inputs with kink == 0, violating this rule.

For any SlopeData input where kink == 0 the reference contract always reverts (setSlopes is rejected) while the mutant accepts at least one such input; therefore calling setSlopes with a fuzzed SlopeData must fail exactly when kink == 0 on the reference implementation.

For every input SlopeData the reference C either reverts when kink == 0 or, if it accepts (kink != 0 and <1e27), then the stored slopeData for that asset has kink != 0; the mutant accepts and stores slopeData with kink == 0 for some inputs, violating that the contract never stores a slope with kink == 0.

For any input slope.kink in (0, 1e27) the reference's setSlopes accepts (does not revert) and stores the slopes; the mutant rejects those valid kinks (reverts) because it inverted the comparison, so there exist fuzzed kink values in (0,1e27) that make the mutant revert while the reference succeeds.

For every nonzero kink < 1e27 the reference contract accepts setSlopes (does not revert) and stores the slopes, while the mutant inverts the comparison and will revert for some of those kink values, so attempting to call setSlopes with a fuzzed kink in (0,1e27) should always succeed on the reference but can fail on the mutant.

For any nonzero kink < 1e27, the reference contract accepts setSlopes (does not revert) and stores the slopes; the mutant inverts the comparison and will revert for such kink values, so calling setSlopes with a fuzzed SlopeData having 0 < kink < 1e27 always succeeds on the reference but may fail on the mutant.

For every nonzero kink less than 1e27, the reference accepts (does not revert on) setSlopes and stores the provided slopes; the mutant inverts the comparison and will reject some of those kinks (revert), so a call with 0 < kink < 1e27 always succeeds on the reference but can fail on the mutant.

For any nonzero kink < 1e27, the reference C accepts setSlopes (call does not revert) and stores the slopes; the mutant inverts the comparison and will revert for some such kink values, so calling setSlopes with a fuzzed SlopeData having 0 < kink < 1e27 should always succeed on the reference but can fail on the mutant.

For every input slopes struct, the reference contract reverts (rejects) when slopes.kink == 0 or slopes.kink >= 1e27, while the mutant accepts such invalid kink values; thus the reference never stores invalid kink values but the mutant may.
